title: WHEN THE MAN BEHIND THE PULPIT HAS MORE THAN ONE WIFE
paragraphs: WHEN THE MAN BEHIND THE PULPIT HAS MORE THAN ONE WIFE
Some Preachers Call Multiple Wives a “Reward From God.” But What Does Scripture Actually Say—and What Should You Do If This Is Your Church?
Imagine sitting in church one Sunday.
The worship is powerful. People are lifting their hands. The preacher opens his Bible. He speaks confidently about holiness, obedience, blessing, marriage, family, and the favor of God.
Then you discover something that makes your stomach tighten.
Your pastor has more than one wife.
Not a complicated past before coming to Christ. Not a deceased wife followed by remarriage. Not merely a rumor circulating among disgruntled members.
Multiple living wives at the same time.
And when someone questions it, the answer is not repentance.
It is celebration.
“God blessed me with these women.”
“Look at Abraham.”
“Look at Jacob.”
“Look at David.”
“Having several wives proves God has favored me.”
Perhaps you have heard something like this.
And now you are confused because the man saying it can preach.
He knows Scripture.
People respect him.
Maybe people call him “Papa,” “Prophet,” “Apostle,” or “Man of God.”
Perhaps miracles are attributed to his ministry. Maybe the church is growing. Maybe thousands follow him.
So you quietly wonder something you are almost afraid to say aloud:
What if he is right?
And if he is wrong...
what am I supposed to do?
Before answering, we need to establish something that can save Christians from enormous spiritual confusion:
The Bible recording something is not the same thing as the Bible recommending it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
Scripture records adultery.
That does not sanctify adultery.
Scripture records drunkenness, betrayal, incest, idolatry, deception, violence, and catastrophic human failure.
The Bible is brutally honest about fallen humanity.
And yes—the Old Testament records men having multiple wives.
Abraham had relationships with Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon's marriages multiplied on an extraordinary scale.
But there is a dangerous way of reading Scripture that says:
“A biblical character did it, therefore God approves of it.”
Follow that method consistently and the Bible becomes a weapon for justifying almost anything.
The better question is not merely, “Did someone in the Bible do this?”
The question is:
“What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about God's design?”
Go backward.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational pattern: a man leaves father and mother, is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Then something remarkable happens centuries later.
Jesus Himself reaches back to that creation account when teaching about marriage.
He does not point His listeners to Solomon's household as the model.
He points them back to the beginning.
Christ speaks of the Creator making humanity male and female, and of a man being joined to his wife so that “the two” become one flesh.
The emphasis matters.
Jesus directs the conversation toward God's creational design rather than using the broken marital histories of Old Testament figures as the standard.
And even Israel's kings were specifically warned:
“He shall not multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
That warning becomes painfully visible in Solomon's story. The accumulation of wives is not presented as a trophy proving spiritual maturity.
It becomes part of his tragedy.
But now we come even closer to the question you are actually asking.
Because your question is not simply:
“Did anyone in the Old Testament practice polygamy?”
Your question is:
“Can a Christian pastor have multiple wives and call them God's reward?”
That question brings us directly into the New Testament qualifications for church leadership.
Paul writes concerning an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:2 that he must be above reproach and describes him with the Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, the expression carries the sense of “a man of one woman,” commonly rendered “the husband of one wife.” Some translations express the ethical force as being “faithful to his wife.”

Paul uses substantially the same qualification when discussing elders in Titus 1:6. The text again presents the elder as ἑνὸς? No—the relevant construction is again the “one-woman man” idea reflected in translations such as “husband of one wife,” while some translations render its force as faithfulness to his wife.
Christians have debated some details of this phrase.
Does it exclude remarriage after widowhood?
What about a man divorced before conversion?
How should churches evaluate complicated histories after genuine repentance?
Faithful Christians do not agree on every one of those pastoral questions.
But those debates should not be used to erase what is unmistakable about Paul's picture of an overseer.
The pastor is supposed to demonstrate sexual and marital faithfulness.
He is supposed to be above reproach.
His household is supposed to reinforce rather than contradict his ministry.
He is not given a special sexual privilege because he has a pulpit.
Pastoral authority does not lower God's standard.
It intensifies accountability.
And that is why describing the accumulation of wives as a spiritual “reward from God” creates such a serious problem.
Where does the New Testament promise pastors additional wives as a reward for obedience?
It doesn't.
Where does Jesus tell faithful ministers that multiple wives are evidence of divine favor?
He doesn't.
Where do the apostolic qualifications for elders celebrate multiplying wives?
They don't.
Instead, the New Testament presents marriage through a breathtakingly Christ-centered picture.
Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Notice the direction.
Biblical marriage is not supposed to display a man's appetite.
It is supposed to display Christ's sacrifice.
Jesus does not exploit His bride.
He dies for her.
He does not use spiritual authority to satisfy Himself.
He gives Himself.
The cross therefore destroys one of the ugliest distortions of spiritual leadership:
the idea that greater authority gives a man greater permission to indulge himself.
Jesus reveals the opposite.
Greater authority means greater service.
The King wears a crown of thorns.
The Lord kneels to wash feet.
The Bridegroom gives His body for His bride.
That is the Man standing behind every Christian pastor.
Jesus Christ.
And every preacher eventually has to answer to Him.
Maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you are reading this while attending exactly this kind of church.
Maybe you love the people there.
Maybe your children have friends there.
Maybe that church helped you when nobody else did.
Maybe you came to Christ there.
Maybe the pastor prayed with you during one of the darkest nights of your life.
Maybe leaving feels like betrayal.
Maybe questioning him feels like questioning God.
Listen carefully.
A pastor can teach you something true and still later require biblical correction.
A church can contain genuine believers while its leadership embraces serious error.
And acknowledging something wrong does not require pretending everything you ever experienced there was fake.
Your ultimate loyalty was never supposed to belong to a preacher.
It belongs to Jesus.
There is only one Christ.
Your pastor did not die for your sins.
Your denomination did not carry your cross.
Your church founder was not raised from the dead for your justification.
Jesus was.
That means the question is not simply:
“Do I like this pastor?”
Nor:
“Has this ministry helped me?”
Nor:
“Is the church growing?”
Nor even:
“Can this man preach powerfully?”
The question becomes:
Is what is being taught consistent with Scripture, and is the leadership willing to submit to Scripture when challenged?
That last question is crucial.
Do not leave a church merely because somebody posted an accusation on social media.
Do not destroy someone's reputation because of gossip.
Verify what is actually true.
Listen carefully.
Examine the teaching in context.
Look at the man's actual marital situation.
Ask whether responsible elders know about it.
If appropriate and safe, seek clarification through mature church leadership.
Bring Scripture—not rumors.
And watch what happens when Scripture confronts power.
That response can reveal a great deal.
If a pastor is discovered in serious sin and responds with brokenness, repentance, accountability, and submission to biblical discipline, that is one situation.
Repentance does not automatically erase every consequence or restore someone immediately to pastoral office. Leadership qualifications still matter.
But repentance matters enormously because Christianity is built around grace for sinners who turn to Christ.
The Gospel Warrior message cannot become:
“Bad people are beyond hope.”
If that were the Gospel, every one of us would be finished.
The message is:
Christ saves sinners.
Christ forgives sinners.
Christ changes sinners.
Christ restores broken people.
But grace never requires us to rename darkness as light.
Repentance means turning.

That is why an openly polygamous pastor who teaches that multiplying wives is a divine reward presents a very different situation from a broken man confessing sin and submitting himself to correction.

When leadership openly celebrates what Scripture's pastoral qualifications contradict, refuses meaningful accountability, and teaches the congregation to accept that contradiction as God's will, remaining under that teaching deserves serious reconsideration.

Paul did not tell churches that sexual conduct becomes irrelevant when the guilty person is influential. In 1 Corinthians 5, he rebuked a congregation for tolerating serious sexual immorality and even condemned their pride about the situation.
So should you leave?
Do not make the decision from panic.
Do not make it from gossip.
Do not make it because someone online told you to become suspicious of every pastor.
But neither should fear of a charismatic leader imprison your conscience.
Test what you are being taught by Scripture.
Seek counsel from mature, biblically trustworthy Christians outside the leader's immediate circle if necessary.
Look for genuine accountability.
Look for repentance.
Look at whether Scripture is allowed to correct the pastor—or whether the pastor has become the person who is allowed to correct Scripture.

And if the leadership knowingly persists in teaching serious error, protects it from biblical correction, celebrates it rather than repenting of it, and demands that members violate their conscience in order to defend the leader, then finding a biblically faithful congregation where Christ and His Word stand above personalities can be a wise and responsible course.
Leaving an unhealthy church does not mean leaving Jesus.
Sometimes following Jesus requires refusing to make an idol out of the person who introduced you to Him.
But there is another danger here.
Do not read this article merely to collect ammunition against somebody else's pastor.
Because the Word of God has an uncomfortable habit.
While we are pointing it at somebody else...
it turns around and searches us.
Maybe your scandal is not polygamy.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe yours lives in browser history.
Maybe it sleeps inside bitterness.
Maybe it hides inside secret messages.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe greed.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe spiritual hypocrisy.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are doing wonderfully while inside you know you are slowly drifting away from Jesus.
Then hear the Gospel before you hear another word of judgment.
Jesus did not come only for respectable sinners.
He came for real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People whose lives became complicated because of choices they desperately wish they could undo.
People who ruined things.
People who were ruined by others.
People who have stood in church smiling while their souls were bleeding.
People who know what it feels like to whisper:
“Jesus... if You still want me, I need You.”
He still calls sinners to repentance.
And His grace is not permission to continue hiding.
His grace is the open door home.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps saying:
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to theological gymnastics.
Not from scandal to pretending sin never happened.
From scandal...
to grace.
And grace takes us through repentance.
Through confession.
Through truth.
Through the cross.
Until the person who once defended darkness can finally stand in the light and say:
“I was wrong. Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That sentence may contain more spiritual power than a thousand sermons preached by a man determined to protect his reputation.
If this exposed something in your own heart—not merely somebody else's—be honest.

And if Christ has rescued you from spiritual manipulation, sexual sin, false teaching, or a season when you confused loyalty to a leader with loyalty to Jesus, your testimony may become somebody else's lifeline. Tell it carefully. Tell it truthfully. Tell it without unnecessary gossip—but tell people what Christ has done.
Not because every church controversy requires departure, but because confusion becomes dangerous when emotions are high and Scripture becomes distant.
It doesn't.
Scripture itself commends examining teaching.
And please do not weaponize this article to harass a particular pastor, denomination, family, or congregation. The purpose is not a digital mob.
The purpose is truth, repentance, protection, restoration, and Jesus Christ.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, consider following and supporting this ministry.
It does not make you more spiritual. It does not earn blessing, salvation, or a higher place in God's kingdom.
Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is free.
Sometimes glorifying God looks like putting truth where another wounded person can find it.
Gospel Warrior is not your Savior.
Your pastor is not your Savior.
Your church is not your Savior.
Jesus Christ is.
Follow Him.
Test teaching by His Word.
Refuse to confuse charisma with character.
Refuse to call something God's reward merely because a powerful religious personality says it is.
And when you discover sin—whether behind a famous pulpit or buried inside your own heart—do not run away from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Because the final hope of Christianity is not that pastors never fall.
It is not that Christians never become confused.
It is not that churches never become corrupted.
Our hope is that there is still a throne above every pulpit...
a Shepherd above every pastor...
a Word above every human opinion...
and a Savior whose blood is still sufficient for every sinner who truly comes home.
Remember this when the preacher disappoints you:
Never let the failure of a man behind a pulpit make you walk away from the Man who carried a cross.
